title: Managing the Room
author: Nimish Lad
summary: Nimish Lad draws on Robert Frisch's Who's in the Room? to argue that many leadership failures are really failures of unmanaged meetings, not poor strategy. Rooms are never neutral: without an explicit stated purpose, participants substitute their own interpretations, and what one person expects to be a discussion another later remembers as a decision. Lad walks through the practice of "stage-setting" -- naming the room's purpose, deciding who genuinely needs to be present, and being transparent when someone's presence isn't required rather than offering token inclusion. He extends the framework specifically to education leadership, arguing that middle leaders are especially vulnerable to poorly framed meetings because they must translate unclear senior direction into classroom practice, and that MAT-wide meetings multiply the tension between inclusion and efficiency across multiple schools.
points: Lad's central claim, borrowed from Frisch, is that most leadership struggles are not failures of strategy but failures of unmanaged rooms -- ambiguous purpose, not bad ideas, is what causes conversations to collapse.

His practical fix is explicit stage-setting: naming upfront whether a meeting is for decisions, advice, alignment, or information-sharing, because each answer changes who should attend and what they should expect.
On attendance, Lad argues transparency beats false inclusion -- it is kinder to tell someone "this decision does not require your presence" than to invite them as a token gesture.

He singles out middle leaders as particularly exposed to poorly framed meetings, since they must translate ambiguous senior direction into classroom practice while also representing their teams upward.
quotes: Robert Frisch, in Who’s in the Room (2011), reminds us that many leadership struggles do not stem from poor strategy at all, but from poorly managed rooms.
A "decision-making" meeting dissolves into open-ended talk. A "discussion" meeting is remembered as a decision, until someone reverses it later.
Frisch’s central insight is deceptively simple: managing the room requires being explicit.
Better to say, “This decision does not require your presence,” than to offer false inclusion. Clarity is kinder than token invitations.
Middle leaders, key agents of changes in schools, are particularly vulnerable to the costs of poorly managed rooms.
Because in the end, the quality of leadership is measured not in lofty statements, but in the lived experience of a room.
